newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BP find revives West of Shetland oil rush.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BP find revives West of Shetland oil rush.

text.p: Five years after oil was found in commercial quantities west of the Shetland Islands, British Petroleum Co Plc (BP) has discovered a third field, reviving interest in Atlantic waters and prompting Britain to offer more acres for exploration.
BP said on Monday it found a "potentially commercial volume of hydrocarbons" 100 miles west of the islands on the Atlantic margin during exploration drilling last year.
Suilven, named after a mountain on the west coast of Scotland, lies to the north of the Foinaven field due onstream next month and northwest of Schiehallion which should start pumping by mid-1998.
All three fields were discovered by BP in partnership with Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell.

"It has to be seen as good news. Since 1993... there has been a lot of talk but now there has been another find and it seems quite significant," said James Dyer of Edinburgh-based consultants Wood Mackenzie.
Dyer said the field could be on a par with Foinaven, which has estimated recoverable reserves of 200 million barrels.
"It's significant for two reasons, first because of its size and second because they're going for an extension of the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS)," he added.

Encouraged by BP's success, Britain's Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said it had designated two new blocks north of Suilven for exploration. Bids would be invited "in a few weeks time", it said.

"BP and Shell are also considering further exploration and appraisal options in the area. This will be assisted greatly by the DTI announcement to designate and offer for licensing new block to the north," said Richard Olver, deputy chief executive of BP Exploration.
The blocks, which lie outside an area disputed by Britain and the Faroe Islands, will be offered in open competition but analysts predict a clear-run for BP and Shell.

"Other companies can bid but it's highly unlikely that anyone would be able to put together a better application in the time available than those who are out there already," said Wood Mackenzie's Dyer.
The DTI said BP's find confirmed its belief that there were still important discoveries to be made on the UKCS.

"It is in the nation's interest that our oil and gas resources should be thoroughly and effectively appraised and this new discovery in quadrant 204 demonstrates its rich potential," said Energy Minister Lord Fraser of Carmyllie.
Britain's benign oil tax regime still makes it one of the world's most attractive locations for oil exploration, despite the remote chance of another very big crude find.

The DTI's decision to offer extra acreage in Atlantic waters comes less than a month before the closing date for applications in the seventeenth offshore oil and gas round, mainly covering waters southwest of Foinaven-Schiehallion and in the Rockall Trough west of the Hebrides.
About 26 bids had been submitted by Monday, the DTI said.
The Shetland Islands, home to the Sullom Voe terminal which exports world benchmark Brent Blend crude and will handle Schiehallion oil, welcomed the discovery.
"It's very good news," said Alastair Cooper, divisional manager of resources for the Shetland Islands Council (SIC).
"As far as the Shetland Islands are concerned, the more oil they find the more likelihood of a pipeline coming to land and if that happens we will be bidding hard for it," he said.
Some 1,000 islanders are employed at the terminal.
